title: Waiting in the queue
objectives: Explain price-time priority for limit orders.
Estimate how long a resting limit order waits to fill.

screens.prose: Three buyers wait at the best bid, £100.10. A posted 300 shares first, then B posted 600, then C posted 400. Now a seller sells 900 shares at £100.10.

containers.label: Bids at £100.10, front on the left

screens.question: Tap the buyers whose orders fill.

hints.text: They all bid the same price. What else tells them apart?
A arrived first. How much of the 900 does A take?
A takes 300, leaving 600. B came next and has exactly 600.

feedback.correct: A and B fill; C, last in line, gets nothing.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Serve the buyers in the order they arrived.

byKey.biggest: You served the biggest orders first. At one price the exchange serves the earliest first, whatever the size.
byKey.share: You gave every buyer a piece. Here the earliest order fills in full before the next one starts.
byKey.c: C arrived last, so C waits until A and B are full.

explain.text: A was first, so A fills all 300. B was next and fills all 600. That makes 900, so C gets nothing yet.

screens.prose: You send a **limit order**: buy 200 shares, but pay no more than £100.10. No seller is asking that little, so your order waits with the other bids.

containers.label: Bids at £100.10, front on the left

screens.question: Drag your order into the bids at £100.10.

hints.text: Drag the blue card into the row of bids.

feedback.correct: You join behind C: the newest order goes to the back.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Move your order into the row of bids.

byKey.you: Your order is still outside the queue. Drag it into the row of bids.

explain.text: A new order at a price joins the back of that price's line. Three orders and 1,300 shares now stand ahead of you.

screens.prose: Better prices fill first, and at one price, earlier orders fill first. This rule is **price-time priority**. Your place in the line is your **queue position**.

containers.label: Bids at £100.10, front on the left

screens.question: How many shares must trade at £100.10 before your order starts to fill?

hints.text: Add up the shares of every order ahead of yours.
A, B and C are all ahead of you.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add up the orders in front of yours.

byKey.next: You expected to fill on the next trade. Three orders are ahead of you, and they fill first.
byKey.own: 200 is your own size. Count the shares ahead of you.
byKey.with-own: You included your own 200. Your order starts to fill once the 1,300 ahead are gone.

explain.text: A, B and C hold 300 + 600 + 400 = 1,300 shares. Sellers must sell that many at £100.10 before a single share reaches you.

screens.prose: B changes its mind and cancels all 600 shares.

containers.label: Bids at £100.10, front on the left

screens.question: How many shares stand ahead of you now?

hints.text: Who is still in front of you?
A and C remain ahead.

feedback.correct: A cancel ahead of you moves you up.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add up only the orders still ahead of you.

byKey.unchanged: You kept B in the count. A cancelled order leaves the queue, so you move up.
byKey.only-b: 600 is what B took away. Count what is still in front of you.

explain.text: With B gone, A and C hold 300 + 400 = 700 shares. You did nothing, yet your order moved up. Cancels ahead of you, and fills, are the only things that move you forward.

screens.prose: Later, D joins behind you with 500 shares. Then you raise your order from 200 to 300 shares.

containers.label: Bids at £100.10, front on the left

screens.question: Where does your bigger order stand?

options.text: At the back, behind D: raising the size counts as a new order
In the same place, now with 300 shares
options.why: You kept your place while adding shares. Exchanges treat the extra size as new, so the order loses its time priority.

options.text: Further forward, as a bigger order
options.why: Size buys no priority at one price. Under price-time priority only time does.

hints.text: Would D accept being pushed back by shares you added after D arrived?
Your extra 100 shares arrived after D.
Exchanges treat a size increase as a fresh order, so it goes to the back.

feedback.correct: Raising the size sends you to the back.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about when your extra shares arrived.

explain.text: Raising the size or changing the price resets your place: you go to the back. Cutting the size keeps your place on most exchanges, since it harms nobody behind you.

canvas.caption: Your order, now 300 shares, goes behind D

screens.prose: Back to the first line: A, B and C ahead of you at £100.10. A trade of 300 shares now prints at £100.10.

containers.label: Bids at £100.10, front on the left

screens.question: Did your order fill?

options.text: No: the 300 shares went to A, at the front
Yes: a trade happened at my price
options.why: You assumed any trade at your price includes you. Trades at £100.10 fill the line from the front, and 1,300 shares are ahead of you.

options.text: Partly: everyone at £100.10 got a share
options.why: You split the trade across the line. Under price-time priority the front order takes it all.

hints.text: Who is at the front of the line?
A is first, with exactly 300 shares.
The 300 shares fill A completely. Nothing is left for anyone behind.

feedback.correct: The trade filled A and nobody else.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Serve the line from the front.

byKey.yes: You assumed any trade at your price includes you. Trades at £100.10 fill the line from the front, and 1,300 shares are ahead of you.
byKey.part: You split the trade across the line. Under price-time priority the front order takes it all.

explain.text: The 300 shares filled A in full. Now 1,000 shares stand ahead of you, and you still hold none. A trade at your price is not a fill for you until the line ahead is gone.

screens.prose: Not every limit order waits. The best ask is £100.14, with 500 shares. You send a limit buy for 300 shares at £100.20, above the ask.
screens.question: At what price does your order fill?

hints.text: Is a seller already willing to accept a price at or below £100.20?
500 shares wait at £100.14.
The order trades at once against them, at their price.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for sellers at or below your limit.

byKey.limit: £100.20 is only the most you will pay. The trade happens at the waiting seller's price.
byKey.bid: £100.10 is the best bid. Your order is a buyer that reaches the sellers, so it trades on the ask side.

explain.text: A limit buy at or above the best ask is **marketable**: it trades at once, at the resting sellers' prices. The limit only caps the price. Here 300 of the 500 shares at £100.14 are enough.

screens.prose: A resting buy order fills only after every better bid and every earlier bid at its price. With $Q$ shares ahead of you and trades of $v$ shares on average, your first fill comes after about $$n \approx \dfrac{Q}{v} \text{ trades.}$$ Cancels ahead of you shrink $Q$.
screens.question: Which change keeps your place in the queue?

options.text: Cutting your size from 300 to 200 shares
Raising your size from 300 to 400 shares
options.why: The extra shares arrive now, so the exchange sends the whole order to the back.

options.text: Moving your price up a tick to £100.11
options.why: A new price is a new line. At £100.11 you would be first, but you would pay a penny more and lose your old place.

hints.text: Which change could hurt nobody behind you?
Cutting your size gives up shares; it never jumps anyone.

feedback.correct: Cutting the size keeps your place on most exchanges.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether the change pushes in front of anyone who arrived later.

explain.text: Cutting your size takes nothing from those behind you, so most exchanges keep your place. Raising it or changing the price makes a new order, which starts at the back of its line.

screens.prose: In a busy share you post a limit buy at £100.10. The exchange's feed shows 20,000 shares already waiting there. Trades at that price average 2,000 shares.
screens.question: About how many trades at £100.10 must happen before your order starts to fill?

hints.text: Each trade clears about 2,000 shares from the front.
How many 2,000-share trades clear 20,000 shares?

feedback.correct: About 10 trades, if nobody ahead cancels.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the shares ahead by the shares per trade.

byKey.inverse: You divided the trade size by the queue. Divide the shares ahead by the shares each trade clears.
byKey.next: You expected the next trade to reach you. 20,000 shares are ahead of you.

explain.text: $n \approx 20{,}000 / 2{,}000 = 10$ trades. Cancels ahead of you shorten the wait. If buyers lift the price first, you may never fill at all.

screens.prose: Market makers post bids and asks all day and earn the spread when both sides fill. Many spend heavily on fast systems to be first in line whenever a new price level opens.
screens.question: What does the front of the queue give them?

options.text: Their orders fill first, so they trade more often at the prices they chose
A better price than the orders behind them
options.why: Every order in the line trades at the same price. The front gets earlier fills, not better prices.

options.text: The right to cancel orders behind them
options.why: Nobody can cancel another trader's order. The front only changes who fills first.

hints.text: Do orders in one line trade at different prices?
Think about the 300-share trade that filled only A.
Being first means filling on ordinary trades that never reach the back.

feedback.correct: The front fills on trades that never reach the back.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall what the 300-share trade did to the line.

explain.text: Front orders fill on ordinary trades, back orders often only when a big seller sweeps the level before a drop. So a good queue position is worth real money. Some futures venues match **pro-rata** instead, splitting each trade by size.

ideas: Price-time priority: better prices fill first, and at one price the earliest order fills first.
Cancels and fills ahead of you move you up; raising your size or changing your price sends you to the back.
A limit order at or through the opposite best price is marketable and trades at once, at the resting price.

formula.name: Wait in the queue
formula.note: $Q$ shares ahead of you, $v$ shares per trade on average.

summary.trap: A trade at your price is not a fill for you: it fills the front of the line first.

quiz.prose: At £50.00 the bids queue up as X 1,000 shares (first), Y 500, then Z 2,000. A market sell of 1,200 shares arrives.
quiz.question: How many of Y's shares fill?

widget.label: Y's shares filled
widget.accept: 200: X takes 1,000, then Y takes the last 200.

feedback.correct: X fills 1,000, then Y gets the last 200.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Fill X completely first, then move along the line.

byKey.all: Only 200 shares are left after X takes 1,000.
byKey.none: X takes 1,000 of the 1,200, so 200 reach Y.
byKey.prorata: You split the trade by size across the line. Under price-time priority X fills in full first.

explain.text: Price-time priority fills X's 1,000 first. The last 200 of the 1,200 go to Y, who keeps 300 waiting. Z gets nothing.

quiz.prose: Your bid of 500 shares is third in line at £100.10. You cut it to 300 shares.
quiz.question: On most exchanges, where does your order stand now?

options.text: At the back of the line
options.why: That happens when you raise the size or change the price. Cutting the size harms nobody behind you.

options.text: At the front, as a smaller order
options.why: Size does not buy or lose priority here. Only arrival time orders the line.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether cutting your size pushes in front of anyone.

explain.text: Cutting your size takes nothing from the traders behind you, so most exchanges keep your time priority. Raising it would send you to the back.

quiz.prose: The best bid is £100.10 with 800 shares. You send a sell limit for 200 shares at £100.05.
quiz.question: At what price do you sell?

feedback.correct: The sell is marketable and trades at the best bid.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for buyers at or above your limit.

byKey.limit: £100.05 is only the least you will take. A buyer already pays £100.10, so you trade there.

explain.text: A sell limit at or below the best bid is marketable. It trades at once with the waiting buyers at their price, £100.10. The limit only sets a floor.

quiz.prose: You have 9,000 shares ahead of you at your bid. Then 3,000 of them cancel. Trades at your price average 1,500 shares.
quiz.question: About how many trades before your order starts to fill?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take off the cancels, then divide by the trade size.

byKey.no-cancel: You left the cancelled 3,000 shares in the queue. Cancels ahead of you move you up.

explain.text: After the cancels, 6,000 shares are ahead of you. At 1,500 shares a trade that is $6{,}000 / 1{,}500 = 4$ trades.
